query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX alloys, a more homogeneous, single‐phase microstructure minimizes interfacial stress during high-temperature oxide growth, thereby favoring the formation of a coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C. In contrast, alloys with heterogeneous, multiphase microstructures develop localized stress concentrations at oxide-metal interfaces that promote oxide cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high-entropy alloy in a metallic solid-solution state, either as a homogeneous single-phase or a heterogeneous multiphase structure.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled heat treatments to adjust grain size and phase fraction, creating either a single-phase microstructure or a multiphase microstructure.
generation.conditions: Exposure in a fixed oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructural features at the oxide/metal interface, including phase distribution, grain boundary density, and interface roughness.
generation.mechanism: A homogeneous microstructure promotes even, low-stress oxide growth, leading to a stable and adherent protective layer. In a heterogeneous multiphase microstructure, differences in phase properties lead to localized stress build-up at interfaces during oxide formation, resulting in cracks and subsequent spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with a refined, single-phase microstructure will develop continuous, slow-growing oxide scales with minimal spallation, while multiphase alloys will display discontinuous oxide scales with visible cracks and spallation upon prolonged exposure above 900 °C.
generation.baseline: A CrFeCoNiX alloy exhibiting a heterogeneous, multiphase microstructure typical of an as-cast state.
generation.boundary: High-temperature operation (above 900 °C) under constant oxidative or corrosive conditions relevant to advanced structural applications.
generation.uncertainty: The relative influence of the specific X element (Si, Mn, or Al) on the stress evolution and exact thresholds for crack initiation are not yet fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiX samples using controlled heat treatments to produce two sets: one with a homogeneous single-phase microstructure and another with a heterogeneous multiphase microstructure. Expose both sets to a fixed oxidative or corrosive atmosphere above 900 °C for an extended duration. Use in situ characterization tools (e.g., high-temperature XRD, electron microscopy) to monitor oxide scale growth, interface stress development, and spallation initiation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and growth rate
Continuity and adhesion of the oxide layer (using surface profilometry and microscopy)
Interface roughness and grain boundary analysis at the oxide/metal junction
Residual stress measurements within the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the single-phase and multiphase samples exhibit statistically similar oxide scale integrity and minimal spallation under identical conditions, for example, similar oxide thickness, continuity, and negligible interface stress differences, then the hypothesis that microstructural homogeneity governs oxide stability is falsified.

In situ thermal observations of materials with the high-temperature XRD provide unique information such as temperature-dependent phase transformations, types of new phase formation, and the start and finish temperatures of competing phases in an alloy system []. In situ HTXRD is instrumental in revealing the real-time of oxide formation as well as the type and temperature at which various kinds of oxide form when metals are exposed to high temperatures in air or in another simulated environment. Our HTXRD analysis provided insight into the thermal stability, phase transitions, and high-temperature oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy samples, which provides significant guidance in the development of high-performance alloys for demanding applications. The surface and cross-sectional microstructure, elemental distributions, and oxide compositions have been examined to further understand the evolution of the oxides. AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. AbstractOxidation behavior of a refractory AlNbTiVZr0.25 high-entropy alloy at 600–900 °C was investigated. At 600–700 °C, two-stage oxidation kinetics was found: Nearly parabolic oxidation (n = 0.46–0.48) at the first stage, transitioned to breakaway oxidation (n = 0.75–0.72) at the second stage. At 800 °C, the oxidation kinetics was nearly linear (n = 0.92) throughout the entire duration of testing. At 900 °C, the specimen disintegrated after 50 h of testing. The specific mass gains were estimated to be 7.2, 38.1, and 107.5, and 225.5 mg/cm2 at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h, and 900 °C for 50 h, respectively. Phase compositions and morphology of the oxide scales were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). It was shown that the surface layer at 600 °C consisted of the V2O5, VO2, TiO2, Nb2O5, and TiNb2O7 oxides. Meanwhile, the scale at 900 °C comprised of complex TiNb2O7, AlNbO4, and Nb2Zr6O17 oxides. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr2Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO4-VO oxides mixture. Earlier works reported that Fe in RM(Nb)ICs had an effect on the formation of Ti-rich Nbss only when it was in synergy with Cr and 5 at.% Sn (alloy NV5). Nbss was not stable when Al and 5 at.% Sn were in synergy (alloy ZX6), when Hf and 5 at.% Sn were simultaneously present with Al (alloys EZ5 and EZ8) and when Fe was in synergy with 5 at.% Sn with/without Cr (alloys NV5 and NV8). In other words, 5 at.% Sn and specific solutes from the group of the elements Al, Cr, Fe and Hf can support or suppress (1) the formation of Ti-rich Nbss in cast RM(Nb)ICs and (2) the stability of Nbss in the alloys. The data for alloy NV2 would suggest that, with 5 at.% Sn, the concentrations of Al, Fe, Hf, Si and Ti in RM(Nb)ICs could be key for the formation of Ti-rich Nbss and the stability of Nbss.

Alloys used in extreme environments, such as turbines and aero-engines, require excellent high-temperature strength and oxidation resistance. Recent progress in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which have five or more elements present in near-equimolar proportions, has resulted in several alloys with excellent high-temperature strength. However, the oxidation and corrosion behavior of HEAs is still poorly understood and modeled. Oxidation is an extremely complex process where kinetics, thermodynamics, and microstructure play a competing role in forming the passivating oxide layer, which prevents a catastrophic oxidation [,]. Challenges in modeling the oxidation behavior of HEAs are numerous, including understanding the role of chemistry, microstructure, grain boundaries, associated volume changes, stresses in the oxide scale, and the environment itself, along with the thermodynamic stabilities at elevated temperature and the kinetics of the process. We attempt a piecewise approach toward modeling the oxidation behavior of HEAs and to address a critical question in this work—how do the composition and the microstructure affect the oxidation behavior of the HEAs? decision.trend: Early work (PMC6513993, 2019) on refractory-based high-entropy alloys (e.g., CrTaO4-protected alloys) demonstrated that certain compositions can form stable oxide scales at elevated temperatures, yet others showed long-term failures via spallation under continued oxidation. Later, investigations of a Cr–Mn–Fe–Co high-entropy alloy (PMC8346963, 2021) revealed that although surface spinel-type oxides initially formed at 700–900 °C, the oxide layer ultimately developed cracks and spalled when exposed to 900 °C for prolonged periods. Despite progress in identifying protective phases, a comprehensive mechanistic explanation for why certain oxide scales remain stable and others fail, especially for CrFeCoNi-based compositions, remains incomplete.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear how microstructural traits—including phase distribution, interfacial stresses, and compositional gradients—govern the transition between stable versus spalling oxide layers in CrFeCoNiX systems, particularly above 900 °C in corrosive or oxidative atmospheres. The interplay among local chemical ordering, diffusion kinetics, and internal stress development in the scale remains unresolved.
decision.lever: Execute a systematic high-temperature oxidation series on single-phase vs. multi-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys—varying grain size and phase fraction via controlled heat treatments—while monitoring real-time oxide growth and spallation under a fixed pO2 environment above 900 °C. Characterize the resulting scales via surface profilometry and cross-sectional electron microscopy to link microstructural features (e.g., interface roughness, oxide thickness, stress) with spallation resistance.
decision.why: Prior studies identified spalling at high temperature, but not the specific mechanistic drivers or how microstructure might mitigate crack formation. This focused experiment directly tests whether controlling constituent phase morphology and associated stress states can stabilize the oxide, addressing the open question of scale stability in high-temperature CrFeCoNiX alloys.
